title: What is static partition pruning (filter value is known at compile time, e.g., `WHERE country = 'India'`) vs dynamic partition pruning (DPP — filter value is derived at runtime from another table, e.g., a join filter, Spark 3.0+)?
shortTitle: Static partition pruning vs dynamic partition pruning (DPP)

s1_definition.profdef: Static partition pruning happens when the filter value on a partition column is a literal known at plan time, such as `WHERE branch = 'Mumbai'`, so the Catalyst Optimizer can decide which directories to read before the job runs. Dynamic partition pruning, introduced in Spark 3.0, handles the case where the filter value is not a literal but is derived at runtime from another table in a join — Spark first evaluates the small dimension side, extracts the distinct join-key values, and injects them as a runtime filter on the large partitioned fact table so it prunes directories even though the values were unknown at plan time.
s1_definition.analogy: Static pruning is when the auditor at the National Bank of India walks in and says "give me the Mumbai drawer" — the clerk knows exactly which drawer immediately. Dynamic pruning is when the auditor says "give me the branches on this list I'm holding," but the list is inside a sealed envelope that only gets opened during the audit. Spark opens the small envelope first, reads which branches it names, and only then knows which large drawers to pull — pruning them at runtime instead of up front.
s1_definition.oneliner: Static pruning uses a literal known at plan time; dynamic pruning derives the pruning values at runtime from the other side of a join.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Static partition pruning happens when the filter value on a partition column is a literal known at plan time, such as `WHERE branch = 'Mumbai'`, so the Catalyst Optimizer can decide which directories to read before the job runs. Dynamic partition pruning, introduced in Spark 3.0, handles the case where the filter value is not a literal but is derived at runtime from another table in a join — Spark first evaluates the small dimension side, extracts the distinct join-key values, and injects them as a runtime filter on the large partitioned fact table so it prunes directories even though the values were unknown at plan time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Static pruning is when the auditor at the National Bank of India walks in and says "give me the Mumbai drawer" — the clerk knows exactly which drawer immediately. Dynamic pruning is when the auditor says "give me the branches on this list I'm holding," but the list is inside a sealed envelope that only gets opened during the audit. Spark opens the small envelope first, reads which branches it names, and only then knows which large drawers to pull — pruning them at runtime instead of up front.

**One line to remember:** Static pruning uses a literal known at plan time; dynamic pruning derives the pruning values at runtime from the other side of a join.

sections.s2_technical:
Static partition pruning is the simpler and older behaviour. When your query says `WHERE txnDate = '2026-10-30'` and the fact table is partitioned by txnDate, Catalyst sees a literal and immediately restricts the file listing to that one directory. The decision is made while building the physical plan, before any data is read. This has existed for a long time and is the everyday benefit of partitioning.

Dynamic partition pruning solves a case that static pruning cannot. Consider a star-schema query: a large fact table `transactions` partitioned by `branchId`, joined to a small dimension table `branches` with a filter like `branches.region = 'West'`. The set of branch ids in the West region is not a literal — it is computed from the dimension table. Without DPP, Spark would read every partition of the huge fact table and only drop rows after the join. With DPP, Spark first runs the small, filtered dimension side, collects the distinct join-key values (the West-region branch ids), and injects them as a dynamic filter on the partition column of the fact table. The fact scan then reads only the matching partitions.

The mechanism relies on the join being a broadcast-eligible or otherwise cheap dimension side, because Spark needs the dimension result early. It is controlled by `spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled`, which is on by default in Spark 3.0 and later. The partition column of the fact table must be the join key (or functionally related to it) for DPP to apply. You can confirm it fired by looking at the physical plan for a `dynamicpruning` subquery expression on the fact scan.

A senior-level nuance is that DPP is one of the biggest real-world speedups for data-warehouse-style joins, often turning a full fact-table scan into reading a handful of partitions. But it only helps when the fact table is partitioned on the join key and the dimension filter is selective. If the dimension yields most of the key values, pruning saves little, and if the fact table is not partitioned on the join key, DPP cannot apply at all.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a huge `transactions` fact table partitioned by branch, and a small `branches` dimension table. A report asks for all transactions in West-region branches. The region is on the dimension, not the fact, so the branch ids to read are unknown until the dimension is evaluated. This is exactly what dynamic partition pruning solves — Spark evaluates the filtered dimension first and injects the resulting branch ids as a runtime partition filter on the fact table.

Problem 2 — A different report asks for transactions in branch Mumbai directly. Here the value is a literal, so static pruning applies and Spark knows the directory at plan time. Contrasting the two shows when each kicks in.

The demo models the fact-table partitions, a small dimension with a region filter, derives the matching branch ids at runtime, and prunes the fact partitions dynamically, logging which partitions are read versus skipped and comparing against the static case.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a fact table with four branch partitions (BR-MUM 1200 MB, BR-PUN 800 MB, BR-DEL 1000 MB, BR-CHE 700 MB) and a dimension mapping branches to regions.

Step 1: For the static case, the query filters on the literal branch id BR-MUM. The pruner immediately keeps only that partition and skips three, reading 1200 MB. The decision needs no runtime information.

Step 2: For the dynamic case, the query filters the dimension on region equals West. The branch ids are not literals, so Spark first evaluates the dimension and derives the set of West branch ids, which are BR-MUM and BR-PUN.

Step 3: Spark injects those derived ids as a runtime filter on the fact table's partition column and prunes, keeping BR-MUM and BR-PUN and skipping BR-DEL and BR-CHE.

Step 4: The dynamic scan reads 2000 MB instead of the full 3700 MB, saving 1700 MB. The demo logs the derived keys, the partitions read, and the bytes saved.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:26:40 [INFO] STATIC prune (branchId='BR-MUM'): read 1200 MB, skipped 3 partitions
2026-10-30 04:26:40 [INFO] DPP derived branch ids from dimension at runtime: [BR-MUM, BR-PUN]
2026-10-30 04:26:40 [INFO] DYNAMIC prune (region='West'): read 2000 MB across 2 partitions, saved 1700 MB vs full scan
2026-10-30 04:26:40 [INFO] Static knew the value at plan time; DPP learned it from the dimension at runtime.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  STATIC:  WHERE branchId = 'BR-MUM'  (literal at plan time)
    │ Catalyst prunes immediately
    ▼
  read only BR-MUM partition

  DYNAMIC (DPP):  transactions JOIN branches WHERE region='West'
    │
    ├─ Step A: evaluate SMALL dimension side first
    │     branches.filter(region='West') → {BR-MUM, BR-PUN}
    │
    ▼ inject derived keys as runtime filter
  fact scan prunes using {BR-MUM, BR-PUN}
    ├─ read BR-MUM   read BR-PUN
    └─ skip BR-DEL   skip BR-CHE
    ▼
  join only the surviving partitions
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Both forms of pruning skip partition directories on the large table, but they differ in when the pruning value is known. Static partition pruning applies when the filter value is a literal that the optimizer can see while building the plan, such as filtering on branch equals Mumbai. Catalyst decides which directory to read before the job even starts, which is the everyday benefit of partitioning on a column you filter with constants.

Dynamic partition pruning, added in Spark three, handles the star-schema case where the filter value is not a literal but is derived from another table in a join. Imagine a huge transactions fact table partitioned by branch, joined to a small branches dimension filtered on region equals West. The set of West branch ids is unknown until the dimension is evaluated. Dynamic pruning evaluates the small dimension side first, collects the distinct join-key values, and injects them as a runtime filter on the fact table's partition column, so the fact scan reads only the matching partitions instead of everything.

In my reporting work at the National Bank of India this was one of the biggest speedups we got for free. A regional report joined a terabyte-scale transaction table to a tiny branch dimension, and before Spark three it scanned the whole fact table and dropped rows after the join. With dynamic partition pruning enabled, Spark derived the handful of branch ids for the requested region and pruned the fact table down to just those partitions, cutting the scan dramatically. The requirements I always mention are that the fact table must be partitioned on the join key and the dimension filter must be selective, and I verify it actually fired by checking the physical plan for a dynamic-pruning subquery on the fact scan. So in short, static pruning uses a constant known at plan time, and dynamic pruning learns the values at runtime from the other side of the join.
